name: Laos
summary: Independent from France in 1953; the most heavily bombed country per person (US bombing, 1964–73); a communist state since 1975.

terrain.value: Rugged mountains and plateaus, such as the Annamite Range and the Plain of Jars, with lowlands along the Mekong.

climate.value: Tropical monsoon: a rainy season from about May to October and a cooler dry season from November to April.

resources.value: Rivers for hydropower, copper and gold mines, timber and fertile rice land along the Mekong valley.

disasters.value: Floods and the deadly unexploded bombs left from the 1960s–70s war; a dam collapse in Attapeu killed dozens in 2018.

population.value: 7,545,800 in a mid-2023 estimate (7,769,819 in a 2024 estimate in the text); 6,492,228 at the 2015 census.

urbanisation.value: Mostly rural, though towns are growing; about a third of people live in towns such as Vientiane, Savannakhet and Pakse.

disease.value: Malaria, dengue and child malnutrition remain problems, though life expectancy has risen strongly since the 1980s.

migration.value: After 1975 roughly a tenth of the population fled, including many Hmong who went to camps in Thailand and later to the USA.

economicBase.value: Subsistence agriculture is about half of GDP and 80% of jobs (rice on about 80% of arable land); more than 540 mineral deposits are known; about 8,000 MW of about 18,000 MW hydropower potential is committed for export to Thailand and Vietnam.

tradeRoutes.value: The Laos–China railway from Vientiane to Kunming (2021) and Mekong bridges to Thailand link the landlocked country.

wealth.value: A lower-middle-income country with heavy public debt, much of it owed to China for dams and the railway.

moneyAndTax.value: The kip is the currency; it lost much of its value in 2022–23, causing high inflation and price rises.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A communist state in which the Lao People’s Revolutionary Party is the founding and ruling party with a legal monopoly on state power.

keyRulers.value: Kaysone Phomvihane led the Pathet Lao government when the country was renamed in 1975; the page does not mention Souphanouvong. Later and present leaders are not named here.

succession.value: Leaders are chosen within the ruling party at its congresses every five years, then confirmed by the National Assembly.

institutions.value: The Lao People’s Revolutionary Party and its Politburo, the National Assembly and the Lao People’s Army.

stability.value: The kingdom (1953–75) suffered coups and civil war; the communist state has been politically stable since 1975.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: The Lao People’s Army is small, with mostly older Soviet-era weapons; it has close training ties with Vietnam.

majorWars.value: Independence on 22 October 1953; Lao Civil War 1959–1975 (20,000 to 62,000 Laotians died); King Savang Vatthana abdicated on 2 December 1975; the US dropped more than 2 million tons of bombs on Laos from 1964 to 1973, leaving some 80 million unexploded.

territoryChange.value: Borders inherited from French Indochina; a brief border war with Thailand (1987–88) did not change them.

alliancesRivals.value: A 1977 friendship treaty with Vietnam; China is the largest investor; Laos joined ASEAN in 1997.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: The National University of Laos opened in 1996; school enrolment has risen, but rural literacy still lags behind.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: The Mekong River, Route 13 highway from north to south, the new railway to China and Vientiane’s airport.

religion.value: 66% Buddhist (Theravada), per the infobox and the 2010 figure in the text.

languageWriting.value: Lao, written in its own alphabet related to Thai; many minority languages such as Khmu and Hmong are also spoken.

artsArchitecture.value: Buddhist temples (wats) such as That Luang in Vientiane and Wat Xieng Thong in Luang Prabang; khaen pipe music.

socialStructure.value: Around 50 recognised ethnic groups: the Lao are about half the population, with Khmu, Hmong and many others.

sharedIdentity.value: A Lao Buddhist culture centred on the Mekong, promoted alongside a multi-ethnic national identity.

dailyLife.value: Many families farm rice, eat sticky rice with larb and live in wooden houses on stilts; the temple is central to village life.

ideasReligions.value: Theravada Buddhism and the state ideology of Marxism–Leninism, later combined with market reforms after 1986.

colonisation.value: A French protectorate from 1893, part of French Indochina, with Japanese occupation in 1945, until independence in 1953.

riseSignals.value: French rule from 1893, when the kingdoms were unified under French control; full independence on 22 October 1953 (infobox).

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge. The page does not mention the 1986 reforms or growth rates; it reports a 2025 GDP of about $16.3 billion (nominal), subsistence farming at half of GDP, and over 5 million tourists in 2024.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: On 2 December 1975 the Pathet Lao government renamed the country the Lao People’s Democratic Republic.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
